strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: Coordination among auto-bidders is practically relevant and understudied. The two application scenarios (third-party agents and multi-campaign advertisers) are compelling.

Strong theoretical contributions: (1) Assumption 1 provides necessary and sufficient condition for individual RoS improvement, (2) Mirror-descent algorithms guarantee coalition value improvement without distributional assumptions, (3) Asymptotic optimality result (Theorem 4.2) justifies the simple coordination mechanism.

Rigorous technical analysis: Sophisticated proof techniques (mirror-descent dynamics, virtual bidder relaxation) with careful tracking of individual vs. coalition-level guarantees. High-probability bounds provided.
Comprehensive experiments: Validation on synthetic data (i.i.d. and non-i.i.d.) and real-world iPinYou dataset showing consistent improvements in both utility and value metrics.
Honest limitations discussion: Paper clearly states when results apply (e.g., non-i.i.d. case lacks individual guarantees) and acknowledges necessary conditions.
weaknesses: Assumption 1 not well-motivated: While proven necessary and sufficient, the condition comparing expectations of advantages lacks intuition. Observation 1 says it holds for 'sufficiently large N' with no guidance on practical values. Missing discussion of when/why it fails.

Limited practical applicability: I.i.d. value assumption oversimplifies; real auctions have repeated competitors. I.i.d. outside bid assumption ignores strategic adaptation. Model restricted to RoS constraints. Outside bidders don't respond to coordination.

Asymptotic results without finite-sample analysis: Theorems 4.1-4.2 are asymptotic (T→∞), providing limited practitioner guidance. Theorem 3.1 shows utility gain of T∆/N but convergence rates and finite-time confidence bounds absent.

Non-i.i.d. results lose individual guarantees: Theorem 5.1 only guarantees total RoS improvement, not individual. Theorem 5.2 requires stronger Assumption 2. Weakens claimed robustness when individual performance not guaranteed.

Real-world validation limited: iPinYou experiments use artificial empirical i.i.d. model (sampling uniformly with replacement), acknowledged by authors as suboptimal. Only one dataset family tested. Small coalition sizes (N≤5).

Practical coordination challenges not addressed: How do coalitions form? Are results incentive compatible when utility redistribution needed (non-i.i.d. case)? Privacy concerns about revealing values? Stability analysis absent.

Incomplete mechanism analysis: Paper proposes simple highest-value-bidder mechanism but doesn't compare to alternatives (e.g., alternating bidders). No ablation studies on Assumption 1 violation margins. Negative result (Theorem 3.1) constructs pathological algorithm.

Presentation issues: Assumption 1 lacks intuitive explanation before formal introduction. Notation (·)+ used before definition. Vague tie-breaking specification in Algorithm 2. Inconsistent error bars in figures.
